repo_analysis_summary: jsonl-viewer is a VS Code extension for multi-GB JSONL. LineIndex.build (src/indexer/lineIndex.ts L215-343) does one streaming pass with a byte-by-byte state machine (inString/escaped/depth/lineHasContent) and produces sparse checkpoints every INDEX_CHECKPOINT_INTERVAL=1024 lines (src/constants.ts L15), totalLines/totalBytes, endsWithNewline and record grouping (recordEndLines/recordEndOffsets, kept only when multiline). The sealed benchmark (scripts/benchmark-index-build.mjs) first diffs against an embedded copy of the original loop (edge fixtures incl. raw newline inside string, dangling string/object at EOF, CRLF, empty lines, pretty records, 1/7/64/1000/100000-byte random splits, intervals 1024/1/3, string chunks), then reports the median paired ratio vs the sync reference. Baseline 0.898, target 1.8. Fixture profile measured in a scratch copy: 16.0 MB, 87,725 lines (~191 B/line), 75.2% of bytes are inside JSON strings, 482,296 strings with average body 26.2 B. So string-body scanning dominates. Nothing has been tried yet (iteration 1, empty history). Scratch measurements (Node v24.21, i5-1340P, paired ratio vs reference, 21 runs, every candidate passed a differential check with 1/2/7/64/1000-byte splits and intervals 1024/1/3): current LineIndex.build 0.946 (503 MB/s); sync kernel with switch, per-byte strings and a nextCp counter 1.130; the same plus a tight inner string-skip loop (backslash => i+=2) 1.498 (772 MB/s, best); table+manual 1.424; Buffer#indexOf(0x22) quote skipping with backslash parity 1.055-1.083 (slower: strings are too short, so per-call overhead dominates); hybrid (16 manual bytes, then indexOf) 1.284; dropping record-end pushes entirely (upper bound, incorrect output) adds about 6% (1.284 -> 1.361). Biggest gap: reaching 1.8 needs per-byte cost cut further inside strings (75% of bytes) beyond the tight loop, plus removing the per-line record-array overhead. Caution: a plain indexOf(0x0a) line jump is NOT valid, because a raw newline inside a string must not end a line (fixture 'raw-newline-in-string'), and depth/quote state decides record boundaries. Every byte outside strings still needs classification.

ideas.title: Tight inner string-skip loop (consume backslash+next byte as a pair)
ideas.source: Scratch micro-benchmark exp2.mjs variant 'switch+manual'; reasoning on the fixture byte profile
ideas.evidence: 75.2% of fixture bytes are string bodies (avg 26.2 B). The reference loop re-enters the outer loop for every string byte and tests inString, then escaped, then 0x5c, then 0x22 (L247-251). A dedicated loop `while(i<n){b=buf[i++]; if(b===0x22){inString=false;break} if(b===0x5c){if(i<n)i++; else {escaped=true;break}}}`, entered with `if(escaped){escaped=false;i++}` to carry escapes across chunks, measured 1.498 vs 1.130 for the per-byte version with the same outer code (+33%). It passed differential checks with 1-byte splits, where the escape lands on a chunk edge. Buffer#indexOf(0x22) skipping was slower (1.055) because strings are short.

ideas.title: Move the hot loop into a sync per-chunk kernel / sync iteration for arrays
ideas.source: Measured: current async build 0.946 vs identical logic in a sync function ~1.0-1.13; 'async-wrapped best' 1.313 vs sync 1.284
ideas.evidence: build is `async` with `for await` (L241) and the 100-line state machine inlined in the async function body. V8 optimizes a resumable async function with its locals in the generator context worse than a plain function. Baseline 0.898 is below 1.0 even though the logic is identical. Keeping the scan in a plain sync loop (iterate `handle` with a sync `for...of` when it is an Array/sync Iterable, or call a sync kernel per chunk that keeps state in locals and writes it back once per chunk) removes that penalty. Async input stays on `for await`. The array input handled by the sealed benchmark gains the most. Wrapping the best sync kernel in for-await over 16 chunks cost nothing measurable (1.313), so the penalty comes from where the loop lives, not from the await itself.

ideas.title: Replace `line % interval` with a next-checkpoint-line counter
ideas.source: Code reading L271/L306/L750; scratch variants use `if (line === nextCp) { push; nextCp += interval }`
ideas.evidence: An integer modulo runs on every newline (87,725 per run, plus the EOF path). Comparing against a precomputed nextCp removes the division. All scratch variants used it and matched the reference for intervals 1, 3 and 1024, including the EOF checkpoint at L306 (`line === nextCp`). It is a small gain because newlines are only about 0.5% of bytes. Bundle it with idea 1 rather than measuring it alone.

ideas.title: Lazy record-end storage: count compact records, keep offsets in a growable Float64Array, materialize number[] only if multiline
ideas.source: Scratch upper bound 'table+hybrid NO-REC(bound)' 1.361 vs 1.284 with pushes; code reading L236-237, L275-276, L327-330
ideas.evidence: Each closed line pushes into two regular JS arrays (L275-276). Both are thrown away when !multiline, which holds for the benchmark fixture and typical JSONL. While the file is compact, recordEndLines[k] === k always holds, so skip that push and keep only a counter until the first sawMultiline. At that moment fill 0..k-1 and switch to pushing. recordEndOffsets cannot be rebuilt from sparse checkpoints, so keep it in a doubling Float64Array (offsets can exceed 2^31, so not Int32), and at the end convert to a plain number[] only when multiline. The public type is ReadonlyArray<number>, and tests or the benchmark compare via Array.from/toEqual, so return real arrays. Removing all record writes measured about +6%. This keeps roughly half to two thirds of that.

ideas.title: Single-compare fast reject inside strings (b > 0x5c is never special)
ideas.source: Reasoning on byte values: 0x22 '"' and 0x5c '\' are both <= 0x5c, and lowercase letters in the fixture ('x','y','z', keys) are 0x61-0x7a
ideas.evidence: The tight string loop of idea 1 still does two compares per byte. Most string-body bytes in the fixture are lowercase letters (padding is 'x'/'y'/'z'.repeat(...)), so testing `if (b > 0x5c) continue;` first gives one predictable compare per byte, and the 0x22/0x5c checks run only for b <= 0x5c. Alternatively, one Uint8Array(256) lookup with 0 for ordinary bytes. Not measured yet; expected to compound with idea 1. Unrolling the loop 2x-4x is another option.

ideas.title: Split the outer-state loop by lineHasContent (two-phase line scan)
ideas.source: Code reading L290-292 (default case runs three compares on every non-structural byte)
ideas.evidence: Outside strings (~25% of bytes: digits, ',', ':', keys' quotes), the default branch checks for space/tab/CR on every byte even though lineHasContent is set by the first byte of a compact line ('{'). Once has===true, the remaining outside-string bytes only need dispatch on '"' '{' '[' '}' ']' '\n'. A small Uint8Array(256) class table (non-special => 0) lets the hot path do `if (CLS[b] === 0) { i++; continue; }`. Measured: the table alone was roughly equal to the switch (1.147 vs 1.130 per-byte, 1.424 vs 1.498 with the manual string loop), so the gain must come from removing the whitespace test, not from the table itself. Benchmark both shapes.

ideas.title: Compact-line fast path: per line, check whether depth returns to 0 at the newline
ideas.evidence: Restructure as an outer 'line' loop: scan from line start through strings/structure, and at '\n' with depth===0 && has, do the cheap record/checkpoint step. Only fall to the slow multiline handling (sawMultiline, empty lines, unterminated depth) otherwise. This keeps the per-newline branch tree small and fits idea 4 (counter-only records while compact). Chunk boundaries mid-line must resume the same state, so the kernel must carry depth/inString/escaped/has across calls exactly as now. Rewards depend on the newline frequency (~0.5% of bytes), so expect a modest gain. Main value is code shape for ideas 4 and 6.

ideas.title: SWAR 32-bit scanning of string bodies for '"'/'\' (aligned Uint32Array view)
ideas.source: simdjson-style structural scanning adapted to JS int32 ops (haszero(v ^ 0x22222222) | haszero(v ^ 0x5c5c5c5c))
ideas.evidence: With 75% of bytes inside strings averaging 26 B, testing 4 bytes per iteration could cut loop iterations about 4x inside long strings (e.g. the 200-600 B padding strings, which make up most string bytes). It needs alignment handling, since Buffer subarray byteOffset may be unaligned (benchmark chunks are subarrays of one Buffer at 1 MiB steps, so they are aligned, but string chunks and random splits are not), plus a byte-wise fallback for head/tail and escape parity. Risky and untested; consider only if ideas 1, 2, 4 and 5 stall below 1.8.

ideas.title: Do NOT use indexOf(0x0a) line jumping or indexOf(0x22) string skipping
ideas.evidence: Buffer#indexOf/Uint8Array#indexOf for quote skipping measured 1.055-1.083, worse than the tight loop (1.498), because of per-call overhead on 26 B strings. Jumping between newlines skips quote/brace tracking, which is wrong: a raw '\n' inside an open string does not end a line in the reference (L247-252), and depth decides record boundaries. Listed so planners avoid wasted iterations.
